In this lesson, we will discuss the sampling distribution of the sample variance [MATH: S^2] and explain how this can be used to construct confidence intervals for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
First, consider a random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] of size [MATH: n.] The sample variance [MATH: S^2,] defined as

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2]

Content:
is an unbiased estimate of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
In general, the distribution of [MATH: S^2] is difficult to find. However, if the random sample is taken from a normally distributed population, that is

Content:
[MATH: X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,n,]

Content:
then it can be shown that the sampling distribution of the random variable

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}]

Content:
follows a chi-square distribution [MATH: \chi^2(n-1)] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that the population is normally distributed, but we do not know the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] In cases like this, the random variable

[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}]

follows a chi-square distribution [MATH: \chi^2(n-1)] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom, where

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: S^2] is the sample variance, and

  • [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] can be written as

[MATH: \bigg( \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{blue}b}, \: \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{red}a} \bigg),]

where [MATH: P(X > {\color{blue}b}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] [MATH: P(X < {\color{red}a}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: X \sim \chi^2(n-1).]

In our case,

[MATH: n = 32, \qquad s^2 = 2.56.]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

We are given that [MATH: P(X > \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}48.232}) = 0.025] and [MATH: P(X < \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}17.539}) = 0.025.] As a result,

[MATH: b = {\color{blue}48.232}, \qquad a = {\color{red}17.539}.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] is the following:

[MATH: (((32 − 1) ⋅ 2.56)/(48.232), ((32 − 1) ⋅ 2.56)/(17.539)) = (1.645, 4.525)]

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that the population is normally distributed, but we do not know the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] In cases like this, the random variable

[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}]

follows a chi-square distribution [MATH: \chi^2(n-1)] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom, where

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size,

  • [MATH: S^2] is the sample variance, and

  • [MATH: \sigma^2] is the population variance.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] can be written as

[MATH: \bigg( \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{blue}b}, \: \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{red}a} \bigg),]

and the corresponding confidence interval for the population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma] can be written as

[MATH: \bigg( \dfrac{s\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt{\color{blue}b}}, \: \dfrac{s\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt{\color{red}a}} \bigg),]

where [MATH: P(X > {\color{blue}b}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] [MATH: P(X < {\color{red}a}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] and [MATH: X \sim \chi^2(n-1).]

In our case,

[MATH: n = 37, \qquad s = 1.5.]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

We are given that [MATH: P(X > \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}54.437}) = 0.025] and [MATH: P(X < \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}21.336}) = 0.025.] As a result,

[MATH: b = {\color{blue}54.437}, \qquad a = {\color{red}39.336}.]

[MATH: ((1.5 ⋅ sqrt(37 − 1))/(sqrt(54.437)), (1.5 ⋅ sqrt(37 − 1))/(sqrt(21.336)))|= (1.220, 1.948)]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will discuss the sampling distribution of the sample variance [MATH: S^2] and explain how this can be used to construct confidence intervals for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
First, consider a random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] of size [MATH: n.] The sample variance [MATH: S^2,] defined as

Content:
[MATH: S^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( X_i - \overline{X} \right)^2]

Content:
is an unbiased estimate of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
In general, the distribution of [MATH: S^2] is difficult to find. However, if the random sample is taken from a normally distributed population, that is

Content:
[MATH: X_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), \qquad i=1,2,\ldots,n,]

Content:
then it can be shown that the sampling distribution of the random variable

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}]

Content:
follows a chi-square distribution [MATH: \chi^2(n-1)] with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Confidence Intervals for Variances

Content:
Suppose that a sample of size [MATH: n=26] is drawn from a normal population with unknown variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] After processing our results, we compute an unbiased estimate of the variance in the usual way and get the following result:

Content:
[MATH: s^2 = 4]

Content:
This is an unbiased point estimate of the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] However, it is unsatisfactory because we have no information regarding its reliability.

Content:
For this reason, it's often more helpful to report a confidence interval for [MATH: \sigma^2.] In this case, a confidence interval is an interval of the form

Content:
[MATH: (s^2-E, \: s^2+E)]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: s^2] is our estimate of the population variance, and
- [MATH: E] is some margin of error.

Content:
In addition, we need to give some indication regarding the reliability of our confidence interval. With this in mind, we will construct a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2].

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Constructing a Confidence Interval

Content:
We have the following sample data from our normally distributed population:

Content:
[MATH: s^2=4, \qquad n=26]

Content:
If we define a new random variable [MATH: X] as

Content:
[MATH: X = \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2},]

Content:
then using the result discussed earlier, we have that

Content:
[MATH: X\sim\chi^2(25),]

Content:
where [MATH: \chi(25)] denotes a chi-square distribution with [MATH: 25] degrees of freedom.

Content:
We wish to find an interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: X] lies within. The diagram below shows the PDF for the [MATH: \chi(25)] distribution. The interval we wish to find is also indicated.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dce9b445b23429d60415e4eb52301fb1]

Content:
Here, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are the labels assigned to the interval's endpoints.

Content:
According to our diagram, we have

Content:
[MATH: P(X < a) = P(X > b) = 0.025,]

Content:
or, equivalently,

Content:
[MATH: P(a < X < b) = 0.95.]

Content:
Now, consider the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement:

Content:
[MATH: a < X < b]

Content:
To obtain an expression for the required confidence interval, we solve this inequality for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.]

Content:
Using our definition for [MATH: X,] we have

Content:
[MATH: a <|((n − 1)S^{2})/(σ^{2}) < b; (1)/(b) <|(σ^{2})/((n − 1)S^{2}) < (1)/(a); ((n − 1)S^{2})/(b) <|σ^{2} < ((n − 1)S^{2})/(a).]

Content:
Replacing [MATH: S^2] with the point estimate [MATH: s^2,] we reach the following expression for our confidence interval:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{b} \lt\: {\sigma^2} \lt \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{a }\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
Now, using a percentage points table for a [MATH: \chi^2(25)] distribution, we find that

Content:
[MATH: a\approx 13.120, \qquad b\approx 40.646.]

Content:
Finally, substituting our values for [MATH: a,b,n=26,] and [MATH: s^2=4] into [MATH: (\ast),] we obtain that our [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for [MATH: \sigma^2] is

Content:
[MATH: (2.460, 7.622).]

Content:
Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure.

---

Item 4 — Tutorial: The General Result

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a normal population with unknown variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population variance [MATH: \sigma^2] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \bigg( \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{blue}b}, \: \dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\color{red}a} \bigg),]

Content:
where [MATH: P(X < {\color{red}a}) = P(X > {\color{blue}b}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2} ,] and [MATH: X \sim \chi^2(n-1)] has a chi-square distribution with [MATH: n-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
Finally, by taking the square roots in our formula above, the corresponding confidence interval for the population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: \bigg( \dfrac{s\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt{\color{blue}b}}, \: \dfrac{s\sqrt{n-1}}{\sqrt{\color{red}a}} \bigg).]

---
